subsubtopic: HIRING OF CONSULTANT TO STUDY DEPARTMENT'S ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Liberal Government of Canada is the most adept in the world at setting up smokescreens to hide the real facts from the people. Let us take, for example, the Department of National Revenue. Members of the Progressive Conservative Party have set out case after case which should be corrected, quota after quota which should be eliminated, and principle after principle which should be changed. What does the Government do? Does it examine each, and deal with it? Oh, no, that would be too simple. It hires Woods Gordon to conduct a study of the administration. Instead of spending the relatively few dollars to be fair to taxpayers, the Minister soaks taxpayers again with another bill of a few thousand dollars to pay Woods Gordon.
Why does the Government not pay back the thousand dollars it lost, misplaced, or stole from the new Canadian at Cochrane? Why does it not fire the public servants responsible for three reassessments of the same file, each with a different result? Why is the Minister not replaced, when he told the House that there were no quotas and it has been proven that there were and are?
The Government protects the Minister when it should be protecting taxpayers who have been harassed and abused. The Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have been advised of the National Revenue official who screamed and yelled at a sick lady who had asked for an audit and, in tears, offered post-dated cheques. However, the Department froze her bank account, driving the company into bankruptcy. Will this official receive an increase in pay? He should be fired on the spot.
What the country needs is an election and a Progressive Conservative Government under the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party (Mr. Mulroney), who will evaporate the smokescreens and clean up the mess the Liberals are hiding behind in their camouflage.

subsubtopic: PENALTIES IMPOSED ON TAXPAYERS DUE TO DELAYS IN MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Revenue Canada has struck a new low in its dealings with taxpayers across the country. The Department is using delays in the mail over the Christmas period to levy penalties against taxpayers, when the real culprit is Canada Post.
A-l Bookkeeping of Yellowknife reports that although employer payroll remittances had been mailed into Winnipeg on behalf of clients on or before December 15, 1983, as is its usual custom, at least three client firms have been assessed late payment penalties of some 10 per cent of the amount due, presumably because Canada Post either failed to deliver the mail on time or postmark it on the day of receipt. This is grossly unfair, both to the clients who get stuck with the bill and to the bookkeeping firm which feels that its reputation has been unnecessarily damaged through no fault of its own.
Why cannot Revenue Canada use a little common sense in its dealings with the public? Why does it use every little technicality in the law to squeeze and penalize honest taxpayers? Why is the Minister so complacent about the seedy, money-grubbing tactics of his Department, or is it that he was responsible for their use in the first place?

subsubtopic: REGULATIONS GOVERNING FISHERMEN'S ELIGIBILITY FOR BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 9 the Unemployment Insurance Commission Board of Referees declared that regulations setting special rules of eligibility for fishermen are unconstitutional. Whereas other workers are required to work 10 weeks to be eligible to apply for benefits, fishermen often have to work up to 15 weeks before qualifying. In the case before the Board of Referees, the applicant had worked 9 weeks at a shore job and 5 weeks fishing, for a total of 14 weeks, but was still ineligible.
This is not the first time such problems have arisen over the discriminatory nature of UI regulations for fishermen. Last year the Supreme Court told the Government that it had no right to impose such discriminatory legislation. This was not good enough for the Government, however, and it brought down legislation which reaffirmed its authority to discriminate against fishermen. Now the whole process has been thrown into question again, but the Government still will not accept that it is doing anything wrong. It is appealing the decision of the Board of Referees.
The NDP and many fishermen's groups have been warning the Government for years that such discriminatory practices will not be tolerated in this country, and that it is necessary to take a whole new approach to this issue. How many more court challenges, legal decisions, and fishermen's lobbies will be required before the Government accepts fishermen in the same way as everybody else? When will the Unemployment Insurance Act be amended to bring fairness to Canada's fishermen?

I want to plead in the strongest way I can that he recommend criteria that will be fair and predictable both for the citizens and the Government in the use of third party demands on a citizen's account.
It is wrong to use a third party demand when guilt is only \ presumed but not established. I recognize the Government may have more difficulty in collecting tax if it has to follow the full legal process of establishing proof of tax debt. Nevertheless, the fundamental presumption of law that the vast majority of Canadians take as their first right is that they are innocent until proven guilty. Those who believe they are innocent, and have the intention of establishing that through the processes that are available to them, are in effect condemned as guilty when the message ripples through a small community that Revenue Canada has frozen their accounts. Their credit rating crumbles, the capacity to pay their bills has been smothered, and their self-esteem has been destroyed.
We live in a society where the rights of the individual are expected to be paramount. A democratic government is one where the government is the servant of the people and, therefore, we must always start from the fundamental presumption that no punitive measures can be taken until guilt has been established. Revenue Canada can also cause the effects of guilt without trial by simply calling for reassessment after reassessment after reassessment of a citizen's tax. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not an amazing flipflop. It was an attempt to ensure continuation of an important service to a number of out of the way, small rural communities in western Canada. while asking every other country to open its markets to Canadian goods. If we really want to succeed in this country, we shall have to be competitive. speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on her aggressive and dynamic commitment to the five principles of medicare and to providing health care services at a reasonable fee for the average Canadian. No one can question her sincerity and dedication toward making high quality health care available for all Canadians regardless of age, sex and the region in which they live.
In this debate on the Canada Health Act I would like to put into perspective the role of the medical profession in the health care of the nation, its successes and its frustrations. My initial comments are directed to Members of the House and, to a lesser degree, to the media for much unwarranted criticism of the medical profession. As a member of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons and one who has practised surgery for 30 years, I resent the derogatory and cynical insinuations made by some individuals who are very much uninformed about the complexities of medical practice and kindle public distrust and anxiety by accusing physicians of such practices as performing unnecessary surgery, ordering excessive or unnecessary stays in hospital and desiring excessive compensatory rewards.
Certainly in every profession there are bad apples that give the profession a negative image, but that is no reason or excuse for the continuing harassment of the medical profession as a whole. The violators of ethical medical practice are few. The vast majority of physicians are sensitive, responsible Canadians who are among our most respected and hard-working people.
There is no other profession in the country that is exposed to the constant stress of responsible decision making hour by hour, day by day, year by year. There is no other profession in which its decisions are often linked with potentially horrendous consequences in terms of life or death, partial or complete physical and/or mental impairment; where decisions must be made on the spot without the benefit of other opinions, committee input, briefing by experts or academics; and where someone seems to be constantly watching over one's shoulder, threatening legal action if the expectations of the patient are not fulfilled. The medical profession, by virtue of its ethics, is
Canada Health Act
at the beck and call of every member of the public at all hours of the day, by any citizen who presents health problems either real or imagined.
The tensions to which medical men and women are exposed are difficult to quantify but may be perceived by the higher than average rate of suicide among M.D.s, by the numbers of the profession who tend to seek solace in drugs and alcohol, and by the many family breakdowns resulting from unavoidable neglect by a medical parent in the performance of his or her duties as a doctor. Yet in the past ten years this same group of medical personnel has provided Canadians with the benefits of ever-escalating refinements in technical advances, as evidenced by our diminishing infant mortality rate and the increasing longevity of Canadians.
The general public has shown its respect for the medical profession by voting it in a recent Gallup poll as being the most credible and trustworthy of professions. I should also add that in that assessment politicians and journalists ranked near the bottom of the list. My plea to Hon. Members of Parliament is to temper any anti-doctor rhetoric by recognizing the significant contribution which those people are making to the quality of life and health of all Canadians.
Also I have been disturbed by the lack of precise statistical information and hard data about the medical system on contentious issues which have created debate and confrontation. Many statements leading to controversy are anecdotal impressions and generalizations. I am referring to the accountability of the provinces for the expenditure of federal funds which have been transferred to provincial governments and which should be spent on health care.
I have found it difficult to find an accurate statement of the annual deficits of hospitals, of the number of bed closures, on the length of waiting lists in hospitals in various parts of the country. A great deal of research is necessary, including studies of Canada's changing demographics, in order to provide health care administrators and politicians with factual information on which they can accurately assess funding and planning priorities in allotting health resources.
The federal Government contributes funds to the provinces for health care through cash and tax transfers. However, there is great difficulty in precisely accounting for the government funds which are expended for health care in each province. There should and must be greater accountability for these funds.
What, then, is the status of the health system in Canada? What are the needs for the future? Many people are on hospital waiting lists. The Canadian Medical Association has given a figure of 150,000 nationwide, but what is the source of that information? It seems to be based more on conjecture than precise information.
My own investigation in the City of Hamilton indicated that for the past four or five years there has been constant pressure for hospital beds, but as a result of a computer monitoring of bed availability in all Hamilton city hospitals, there is no real

January 20, 1984
Canada Health Act
problem of bed shortages for emergency cases. For elective surgery, there are a few days of waiting. For non-urgent cases, the average wait is between 30 and 45 days. These figures are approximations, not precise calculations.
Again in the Hamilton area, there are periodic hospital bed closures amounting to 130 beds. These closures are carried out each summer and during the Christmas holidays, but are restored for the rest of the year. The reason given for the temporary closures is a budgetary one. For a variety of reasons, there is greater delay in the assigning of beds to patients for the cardiac ward. The delay is not only due to a shortage of beds as such, but due to an inadequate number of intensive care beds and provisions for diagnostic studies.
As far as the funding of hospitals in Hamilton is concerned, the Province of Ontario had no difficulty in covering operating deficits for our hospitals until approximately three years ago. Since that time many hospitals have been left to their own devices to fully meet their costs.
The lack of capital funding for new medical equipment, renovation and replacement of buildings has been a serious problem. In Ontario, permission to retain surpluses and to use discretionary funds such as those derived from gift shops and local fund-raising campaigns has slightly improved the situation, yet because capital funding is inadequate in all hospital departments, budget restraints are therefore enforced. The situation which I have outlined is that in one area, Hamilton, an urban setting where there is a university teaching program involving community hospitals. These observations can in no way give an adequate overview of the needs of the community style of hospitals in small towns or in different areas of the country, such as the Maritimes or Yukon Territory.
In assessing the needs of our medical system, it must be remembered that there is no single program of medicare in Canada. Instead, there are ten variants. Each province has its regional problems and its own remedies for adequate delivery of medical care.
The health care system in Canada is regarded as one of the finest in the world. This is not an exaggeration. A great deal of credit goes to the administrative skills of both senior levels of government, but the ultimate credit must be given to the health professionals.
The responsibility of providing care in the past 10 to 15 years has become extremely complex and demanding. The reason for this has been an explosion of medical knowledge involving the application of all forms of technical advances in equipment and procedures. This eruption of knowledge and information has necessitated a growth in the need for specialists in medicine in order to apply the new techniques with skill and understanding.
In addition to the traditional expert nursing care, this has led to a generation of new health care technicians; the paramedic, the respiratory technician, nursing aides, otologists, speech therapists, social service workers and so forth. Each specialty and sub-specialty has its own supportive team of technicians. This had led to better medical care, but it has also led to
increased wage costs and increased costs for new medical equipment.
Also, as a result there has been some confusion among the Canadian public as to the role of the different members of the health care team. Many patients do not know the extent of training of many of the health workers and do not appreciate their skills and their limitations. They are uncertain how to interpret the variety of opinions which they have received, some of which appear to be contradictory. Many patients are not prepared to take the assessment of the nursing practitioner, the psychologist and the physiotherapist alone, and this has led to some frustration with our health care delivery system.
Why has there been resistance of some in the medical profession to medicare? The doctor, in whatever field he is practising, has always linked his services to the individual. His traditional contract was solely between the individual and himself. In that way, he was free to make an assessment of the patient's problem and employ his skills as his judgment indicated. The patient, in turn, selected him on the basis of previous medical consultations or the recommendation of a satisfied patient. More recently, however, a third player- government-has entered into the picture and interfered with this traditional one-to-one relationship.
Since government has the power of the purse, there is growing fear that the doctors' autonomy is being eroded and that there exists a potential for stifling his or her freedom to practice according to his or her conscience. Many doctors in Canada look upon this as their principal complaint. They resent any interference with what is deemed to be their right to decide on his or her own fee. However, I should stress that by far the great majority of doctors are practising within the fee schedules agreed to by their profession and the individual provincial governments and they are satisfied with the system, especially as the medicare program has facilitated the collection of fees owed to them and has led to the upgrading of many hospitals.
Some fear has been expressed that a time may come when a physician could be guided by rules and regulations imposed on him or her by the state if all doctors must be opted into government programs and that doctors could be forced to fulfil the financial requirements of the state rather than meet the specific needs of the patient. For example, a rule could be imposed that there would be no kidney transplants for people over 60 years of age because such transplants are not cost-beneficial.
This is an exaggeration, of course, but there have been examples in this century where some states have issued horrendous dictates to medical practitioners. This is one argument, though, which has been advanced in favour of allowing physicians to opt out of medicare. This may be a valid argument in favour of allowing opting out as a safety measure for physicians, but it is not an argument which can be advanced in favour of extra billing.
The very fact that only 2 per cent of doctors' incomes comes from extra billing, while 98 per cent comes from medicare, is lost on many citizens. However, a problem still exists both for
January 20, 1984

patients who do not want to be extra-billed and for many doctors who feel threatened by imposed fee schedules. Indeed, some doctors feel that they have a fundamental right to decide on the fee for service to a patient and that a case could be made for this right based on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The current health care system can be improved considerably from the point of view of the medical profession. To increase the acceptance of our medicare system, doctors should be able to opt out of medicare along the Ontario model, but without extra billing privileges. Allowing doctors to opt out of medicare and yet collect their fees from medicare would let doctors retain their independence in principle and not become civil servants.
Paying all physicians at uniform rates as at present is leading to mediocrity in Canada's medical care. The pay scheme now in existence encourages equal pay for unequal training and experience. Seniority does not count for increased compensation. Currently, operative and medical procedures are paid according to the procedure itself, unrelated to the duration of the procedure or to the physical state of the patient. The system has failed to recognize talented, well-trained, experienced doctors.
However, all of these factors are beyond the jurisdictional scope of the federal Government because the doctors' fee schedules are set by the individual provinces. Because of the jurisdictional separation, the proposed Canada Health Act cannot provide a solution to the fee schedule of the medical profession or a solution as to how that fee schedule should be arrived at.
Doctors are entitled to adequate compensation but as yet no one has defined what is adequate. If merit, experience, and expertise are ultimately to be taken into consideration in arriving at appropriate compensation to doctors, then it is up to the provincial medical associations to draw up a fee schedule and for doctors to then lobby the provincial governments, not the federal Government, to accept that fee schedule.
If physicians, particularly in some specialties, are asked to discontinue extra billing, then a system of fees taking into account the doctors' experience, degree of training, type of community they live in and the complexity of the medical procedure performed must be negotiated with the provinces. This negotiation of fees is referred to indirectly in Clause 12(c) of the new Canada Health Act, but the details of the compensation to be paid to physicians is, as I have mentioned, a matter that must be resolved between the provincial governments and the doctors. A better consultative mechanism between the doctors and each province is needed if doctors are to be satisfactorily compensated and thereby encouraged to stay within the medicare system and eliminate extra billing. Perhaps an amendment should be considered for inclusion in Clause 12(c) of the proposed Act to make it a requirement that a consensus be reached by the provinces with doctors
Canada Health Act
before fee schedules or other changes to the medicare system are arranged.
Canadians as a whole are pleased with medicare. Though the existence of waiting lists to visit a doctor or to enter a hospital is a concern, by and large Canadians are willing to wait for treatment as long as our medicare system provides good medical care on an implied "free" basis. However, many people are displeased with the so-called assembly line or cursory treatment given by some physicians. Such treatment relates more to the personality and to the philosophy of the individual physician rather than to the efficiency of the system. It is unlikely that such physicians would change their practice under another fee structure.
The bed shortage in Canada is aggravated by many situations, such as pressure from patients and their families to remain in hospitals, by an inadequate number of nursing beds and requirements in some provinces that patients must be admitted for certain tests. Utilizing the complete facilities of a hospital for only five out of the seven days in a week is another factor. Yet there is an erroneous public perception, fuelled by the media and some politicians, that the blame for unnecessary hospital admissions should be placed on the doctors.
Canadians are dissatisfied and worried about the incidence of extra billing by doctors. This is especially so in emergency situations. There is a practice now in vogue in using a number of consultants, particularly in cases of trauma but in other emergency cases as well, without consulting the family. Such billing can amount to formidable sums that cannot be handled by low and middle income families.
The needs of hospital care services should be assessed scientifically and projected for the future in order to control costs. The time has come when people expect to have diagnosis made by sophisticated technical devices, such as the costly "Cat" scanners, rather than by exploratory operations.
The assessment of the pros and cons and the costs of various medical procedures and equipment should be presented to the public and a decision should then be made as to whether or not Canadians are prepared to pay increased taxes to meet our hospital care needs. Better use of nursing home care, community health clinics and health promotion programs can keep the hospital population reduced and costs diminished.
Such a change in emphasis must be brought about by the provinces and not the federal Government, as they are responsible for the delivery of the health care system in Canada. Physicians should also be made aware of the prevailing economy and be realistic in their expectations during periods of fluctuations in the economy. In other words, there is a great deal which can yet be done in Canada to improve the efficiency and cost effectiveness of our health care system within the current level of spending.
The increasing number of medical graduates is a luxury which the country may not be able to afford in the future. In 1975 there was one doctor for every 890 people in Canada. In 1981 there was one doctor for every 563 people. Each new doctor in a community increases the costs to the medical

January 20, 1984
Canada Health Act
system, according to different economists, anywhere from $250,00 to $500,000 per year. In addition, their distribution to cover the needs of the country has not yet been solved.
The general public has indicated that they are in favour of having the financial burden of health care carried by general taxation and by premiums rather than by user fees or extra billing by the medical profession. This is the principle of having the population as a whole assume the cost of our medical needs. But there is still a question as to how much individual Canadians are prepared to pay through taxes for health care.
One of the five principles of medicare is accessibility. However, there are anomalies in Canada's size and make-up which in effect tend to result in a violation of the accessibility principle of medicare in the less populated and remote regions of our vast country. There is a tendency for geographic distribution of hospitals and physicians in the highly populated southern section of the country. This problem of accessibility to the highest quality of medical care in the more remote and less populated areas of Canada is one which both the federal and provincial governments should review.
In speaking of accessibility, the term "reasonable and affordable accessibility" should preface that vital principle of medicare.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Hon. Member. It concerns an area which he covered quickly and suggested that it was an area for provincial concern alone. It basically is the position put forward by the Canadian Nurses Association. I believe that all of my colleagues here from British Columbia have been lobbied by the Registered Nurses Association of British Columbia.
There are four points which they have put forward that would reduce the cost of health care and probably provide more effective health care to Canadians generally. The first one is that nurse practitioners and nurses be given the opportunity to provide first access point and that it not be exclusively the right of physicians. Second, the health care legislation should put greater emphasis on prevention and education, or health promotion, as a mechanism for saving. The third point they brought forward is that community health clinics be developed in which health care professionals would work on a community basis. Of course, they have a proven track record in many areas of the country. The fourth point is that there be more emphasis and support federally for community-based health services, such as home care for the chronically ill.
I suggest that the Canadian Nurses Association has put forward one of the most sound responses and suggestions for improving health care in Canada as a basis for the Canada Health Act. Why has the Government and specifically members who are as influential as the previous speaker not come forward in outright support but preferred basically to cop out by saying that this is strictly a provincial responsibility? Why
is the federal Government not providing direct funding as an incentive to allow this kind of thing to happen?

There is a great deal of merit to what the Hon. Member says. At this point, however, we have not really sold the concept of a nurse practitioner to the public as a whole. I am sure the Hon. He would be the very first one to complain that he should have been assessed and treated by someone who is very conscientious, intelligent and dedicated and not someone who really does not have the full experience or background to make the kind of diagnosis he would want.
If we were able properly to sell to the Canadian public the very fine service that nurse practitioners can give and if the program were such that nurse practitioners would work with the appropriate clinical and medical background, I think it would be an ideal way of reducing costs and giving good service. I do not think that society has accepted that concept as much as the Hon. Member and the nurses feel at the present time.
His other question referred to advertising various preventive methods of controlling health and that is a major undertaking. The number of cigarettes smoked each year is increasing, so the effectiveness of that program can be questioned. You can only go so far with the educational techniques and methods we have, because it is the individual's will to accept consultation and advice that counts in the long run.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is particularly desirable when I am on my feet making a speech.
I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act. If I may be permitted a personal reference, my interest in the subject stems largely from a strong family connection with the health care profession. My late father was a surgeon; an uncle, his brother, is a urologist in Charlottetown; my eldest brother is a cardiologist in the same city; a brother-in-law is the public health officer in New Brunswick; a sister is a hospital dietician, and another sister is an instructor of nursing associated with a large hospital in Peterborough, Ontario. But I cannot stand the sight of blood, Mr. Speaker, which explains why I am a politician and not a doctor!
My own views do not merely reflect the interests of the health care professionals. I have made up my own mind on the question before us. I think the Progressive Conservative caucus as a whole has done its homework under the outstanding leadership of the official spokesman for this Party in the field of health, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). Other members of caucus have done a lot of work in the area as well. Among them is the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) who, as Minister of National Health and Welfare in the Clark Government, laid the groundwork for a major review of health under the direction of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall.
I am proud that the new Leader of this Party was so quick to express his support for medicare following his election to that post in June. Indeed, support for medicare was one of his major policies in the Central Nova by-election.
Given the Party's long-standing commitment to medicare, extending back to the Progressive Conservative leadership convention and policy conference in 1956, one can only express puzzlement at the Government's and the media's surprise that Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament would support the Canada Health Act.
While recognizing that the Bill is far from perfect, how could we not vote for, or at least support in principle, legislation of this kind, given our history of commitment to the bases of medicare? After all, it was the Diefenbaker Government which enacted the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act in the late 1950s. That legislation, which extended access to hospital coverage on a prepaid basis to all Canadians, was a precursor to medicare and is now to be superseded by the legislation being debated today.

January 20, 1984
Canada Health Act
The same Diefenbaker Government established the Royal Commission on Health Services headed by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, reflecting the intent of the government of the day to launch a national medical insurance plan. When the succeeding Liberal Government in 1966 sponsored the Medical Care Act based on Mr. Justice Hall's report, every single Progressive Conservative Member of Parliament without exception, to my knowledge, voted for it. Our Party's support for the principles of medicare-universality, accessibility, portability, comprehensiveness, and public non-profit administration-has not flagged since that time. Why, then, I ask you, Sir, should anyone be surprised by the position which the Party is taking on Bill C-3?
This Bill seeks to do several things. Essentially it details the conditions under which federal payments will be made to the provinces for insured health services. Basic to those conditions is the Government's opposition to extra billing and user charges by doctors and hospitals. The Bill authorizes the federal Government to reduce payments to a province by the amount of extra billing or user fees it charges.
As far as my own Province of Prince Edward Island is concerned and the Atlantic region as a whole, this facet of the Bill has little direct relevance, if any, which is an irony because extra billing has been at the heart of the medicare controversy. There is very little extra billing in the Province of Prince Edwaid Island. To the extent that it exists, island doctors are allowed to extra-bill while remaining in medicare. They simply bill the patients directly, then arrange for them to be reimbursed by the plan for the amount covered by medicare. If the charge is no more for a given service than the amount covered by medicare, the doctor can bill the plan directly and the patient never has to pay a single cent out of his or her pocket. In the event the charge for the medical service does exceed the amount covered by the plan, there are flexible arrangements for the payment of the balance.
In practice, Mr. Speaker, few doctors in Prince Edward Island extra-bill. Extra billing tends to be restricted to rare cases where patients request special services beyond normal medical requirements; or even less often, where the fee covered by medicare for a particular service is patently out of whack with its widely accepted value. In fact, each year the total amount of extra billing by the Island's 120 practising doctors is less than $500,000. This is a small sum relative to the $118 million contributed to health care by the federal Government, by the province and by the private sector together. Moreover, Islanders are not charged premiums for medicare, and user fees are not levied at local hospitals. In most of the rest of Atlantic Canada, the level of opting out and extra billing is about the same as that on the Island. In all of Canada, in fact, the amount of extra billing last year was only $100 million, which is a paltry sum in the context of the total national health care bill of $30 billion.
Yet, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), in an effort to latch on to an issue which would shore up the sagging fortunes of the Liberal Party, has talked about
little else for well over a year now. She has treated the issue as though it were not just the most important health question in the country, but the only one. In the process, the real problems which plague the health care system have remained neglected. In truth, Mr. Speaker, the Government's Health Care Act is virtually irrelevant to the conditions of Prince Edward Island and Atlantic Canada as a whole, and I venture to say it is irrelevant to the concerns of most Canadians.
How can you say that?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: It utterly fails to address our most important problem-and this includes the Province of New Brunswick-which is not one of how funds are raised but rather whether funds are available at all for certain types of health care. In Prince Edward Island, for example, and in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, a limited tax base prevents the province from offering a range of medical services which are taken for granted elsewhere-
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
-or from covering under medicare certain types of services which are offered. The plan does not insure- and I direct this to those who say this is nonsense and 1 advise them to check the facts-the plan does not insure such fields as podiatry, optometry and chiropractic-I am talking about my own province in this case-nor are drugs covered, even for senior citizens, as is the case in some other provinces.
The funding problems of Prince Edward Island are compounded by the fact that it has the highest proportion of senior citizens in the entire country. Twelve per cent of the population is over 65 years of age as compared to only 9.5 per cent nationally. At present the age group over 65 years accounts for approximately 42 per cent of all those who use hospital services in Canada. Statistics Canada has documented that, if current hospital capacity and utilization rates remain unchanged, Canadians over 65 will require 71 per cent of all hospital beds by the turn of the century, and every hospital bed in the country by the year 2021. This situation, given current trends, will likely continue to be even more critical on Prince Edward Island than in the country as a whole.
Despite those facts, Mr. Speaker, the Health Care Act before us for debate today remains silent on issues, concerns and problems of that kind. At a meeting with the Health Minister of P.E.I., Albert Fogarty, the federal Minister refused to commit herself to addressing the province's specific concerns. Mr. Fogarty himself has promised to seek support from his counterparts throughout the region so as to convince Ottawa to act. For my own part, I have begun to discuss the matter with Members of Parliament from the Atlantic region in both major parties in an effort to broaden support for Mr. Fogarty's initiatives.
One possibility which is well worth pursuing, and which was alluded to a few moments ago by a representative of the New Democratic Party, is increased utilization of nursing and other non-physician personnel to provide high quality, cost-effective services to all members of the population, especially the aged.
January 20, 1984

Access to the skills and abilities of such personnel is limited in the existing system, geared as it is to traditional physician-based care.
Similarly, more needs to be done to deliver health care services outside the conventional hospital setting. Hospital care constitutes about half of Canada's total health care costs and nearly two-thirds of all government spending on health. Current arrangements encourage some doctors and patients-not all of them but enough to be of concern-to over utilize hospital facilities. Controlling hospital expenditures, therefore, will require incentives to employ non-hospital facilities, including community health centres and home care, where possible.
The author of a superb study published in 1972, Dr. John Hastings, then of the University of Toronto, and 1 believe he may still be there, once said that it would cost less to care for some patients in a first-class hotel than in a hospital without any sacrifice in the quality of service. In P.E.I. about 10 per cent to 20 per cent of acute care hospital beds are tied up by convalescents when these people could just as easily be cared for out of hospital in facilities more appropriate for that purpose and cheaper to service.
Clearly savings can be achieved in all kinds of ways that could free up money for health care objectives. A major emphasis on preventive medicine would serve the same end. At present the system is biased in favour of curing illness rather than preventing it. The priority, Sir, is exactly the opposite of what it should be.
In the final analysis, cost-saving measures must be based on a genuine commitment by government to health care. That truth applies to the federal Government as much as it does to the provinces. While attacking the provinces for the way they are funding their share of health care in Canada, the Minister's own Government has actually been reducing its relative contribution to the system. The Minister engages in statistical sleight-of-hand to prove otherwise. But when preventive and extended health care programs are included in the calculations, the federal Government's contribution to the national health care system is now down to 40 per cent, compared to just under 50 per cent when Established Programs Financing was launched in 1977.

Given the recent potential for further erosion of medicare in Canada, it was urgent that steps be taken to protect medicare. citizen. Health care in Canada today is not better just because we have more and better doctors, just because we have more hospitals or are committing more public funds than ever to this essential service. The Canada Health Act renews a commitment made to Canadians that freedom of access, equality and administrative efficiency would be the hallmarks of publicly financed health services. I would like to speak about freedom of access for a moment. If access to quality health care was not a right, who would be the first to suffer? It would be the poor and the elderly. Who would wish to see a two-tiered system in Canada where one's state of health would be determined by one's financial resources? Poor and rich alike should have equal access to medical care when they are sick.
Federal-provincial financing of medical services has resulted in administrative efficiency as well. Today we have a substantially greater number of physicians and hospital facilities, and a more equitable distribution of both than would have resulted in a health system dominated by private insurance. Having one plan reduces administrative costs, eases the fears of the ill and simplifies the delivery of health services. Voices from the right call for privatization of the Canadian health system, and these same voices attack the Canada Health Act because it proposes Financial penalties for those provinces which allow user fees and extra billing.
We have heard the arguments-user fees deter frivolous use of medical services and extra billing provides an infusion of cash into the national health sytem. I, for one, am tired of listening to those arguments. There is no evidence to support the claim that hospital services are being abused. We know from the report of the Hall Commission that hospital user fees deter the sick, the poor and the elderly from obtaining medical treatment. However, is that what we want? I think not.
Recently the New Brunswick Minister of Health gave a ringing endorsement of user fees by stating that visits to outpatient departments have fallen by 16 per cent since the imposition of user fees in that province. Also the Health Minister announced that the revenue from these fees for the first year should approach some $3.4 million. It is true that people may have been deterred-the poor and the old-but the claims of savings are very suspect. The Government of New Brunswick is operating under a fiscal illusion. Money is saved only if alternate care is not sought. We must then look at the costs of seeking that alternate care or, of greater importance, the costs of forgoing care. In this case lack of treatment could cause serious illness. Indeed this is false economy. Further I remind the Government of New Brunswick that its calculations are based upon a partial study; this its brave estimate of perceived savings presents a shaky argument for regressive fees.
For Canadians the cost of extra billing in 1983 was $72 million. This is unacceptable. Canadians should not have to pay again for a service they have already paid for. The arguments for extra billing are as fallacious as those for user

fees. Without a doubt extra billing discourages office visits, but this is not something to cheer about. Doctors claim they extra-bill because they do not receive adequate compensation for their services. If this is so, why do not all doctors extrabill? The vast majority of doctors have chosen to accept the provincial benefit schedule and do not extra-bill for any of their services. As well, extra billing is more common in provinces where the incomes of doctors are generally higher. There is no evidence that higher pay schedules for doctors deter extra billing. For instance, in Alberta a large fee schedule increase of 15.5 per cent in 1979 had little, if any, impact on the level of extra billing.
Both extra billing and user fees are said to put extra funds into our health care system. This is nonsense. Physicians pocket the dollars from extra billing and, as I have pointed out, user fees are not an effective cost remedy. In fact both these deterrent charges are in reality a public health hazard.
I want to touch briefly on the myth of underfunding. No respected independent health economist in Canada feels that our health care system is underfunded. Earlier this week I heard the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) talk about the "dearth of funds in the health care system". Also I heard his suggestion that both user fees and extra billing are benign responses to underfunding of the system. This type of misinformation adds little to the debate.
I agree with the view of the New Democratic Party health critic that we should look to the future of medicare. I personally envision a health care system based less on large institutions and more on community health centres, home visitation programs and programs of preventive medicine, all of which would complement our large hospital complexes. He spoke mainly of increased funding-and that is typical of that Party-to reform the health system when in fact the modes of delivery of which he spoke are considerably less expensive than traditional delivery systems. Expanded funding alone will not preserve the principles of medicare. A reaffirmation of the federal commitment to medicare, as this Bill surely is, will show our political will is unshakeable. Similarly, I find the views of the Conservative health critic, the Hon. Member for Provencher, that provinces cannot afford to get into alternate care schemes because they are now strapped for funding, to be a misleading argument. I use as an example my Province of New Brunswick where an extramural system of hospital services was begun two years ago. The goals of the program were to reduce demand on hospitals and nursing homes, reduce demand on high-cost, high-tech equipment, reduce home visitations by doctors and expand the roles of nurses, occupational therapists, physiotherapists and dieticians, to name a few. These services allow hospitals to discharge patients early, thereby freeing acute care beds. The terminally ill are often cared for at home in a more comfortable, supportive and familiar environment. The results of the program are admirable. Presently the patient cost per day in

this program is $22, compared with $220 per day in hospitals and $50 per day in nursing homes.

The Liberals have again shown that they are prepared to say anything, do anything, be anything in order to be elected. Once again we have caught them out to lunch. The Liberals failed to realize that John Diefenbaker brought in the original Hospital and Diagnostic Services Act. It was John Diefenbaker and this Party's Bill that set out the five conditions which they laud and parade around the country. It

What we are talking about is $5 billion cash that is raised through this Parliament from all Canadians and then transferred to the provinces for the purposes of health care. We are talking about what are reasonable conditions that Parliament and the elected members should expect in order to be accountable for that $5 billion. We all agree that under the medicare system, which covers both doctor and hospital services, the five conditions are reasonable. We all agree that reasonable reporting and information should come from the provinces. Therefore, we do not have an issue on the points that the Minister has been trying to make.
It is important for Canadians to remember that we are dealing with the cost of doctors and their services, which is about 15 per cent of the overall total cost of health care. We are also dealing with the other 85 per cent which covers hospital costs and the operating and capital costs for the system. It is to that area that we need to direct our attention, particularly for the future.
My first major point is that medicare is universally agreed to. No one disputes the value of it. When we get sick and are not able to work, all we want to concentrate on is getting better. We are prepared to pre-pay, whether by premiums or general taxation, hospital costs. That is a reasonable request.
In terms of social policy, I do not see that as being socialism. My attack against the Liberal Government and the NDP is the way they have socialized the economic creation of wealth. History has taught us for many centuries that it is the individual and the flexibility that individuals give to corporations as well as their entrepreneurial spirit that creates wealth rather than the state trying to do that. That is why we are Progressive Conservatives. In terms of economics, we are Conservatives because we know the individual can do better than Canadair, Petro-Canada or de Havilland. In terms of social policy, there are all sorts of things we can do collectively; for example, our educational system from which we all benefit.
I, along with other Hon. Members, have studied this issue very carefully. I have listened to and talked with many doctors. I have read the views of the provincial governments. I am convinced that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) deserves some genuine and fair criticism for the manner in which she has handled this whole issue over the last two or three years. She has tried to politicize this issue for the benefit of the Liberal Party. That will punish them, as the polls show. People are on to that.
The Liberal Party has been elected too many times by bringing forward issues that appeal to a certain sector and is prepared to write off whole sections of the country. That is not acceptable. People do punish political Parties. In 1968 the Liberal Party had 27 western members. It does not have any in the west now. It is not because there is anything wrong with the Constitution or with the people of the west. It is the deliberate policies which they brought forward.
Is that why you do not have any members from Quebec?

Exactly, and this Party will get its act together, as it is now doing, and will start to get members from Quebec.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare and the federal Government missed a golden opportunity to grasp this whole question of health care and leave medicare stronger for our children and grandchildren. By their fights with the provinces in other areas, whether it was on the first proposal of the Constitution or on the National Energy Program, they have set up a climate of distrust. When people want all of us to work together and handle the medicare problem, it cannot be done. This is because the relationship between the provincial and federal Governments has been too badly injured.
The majority of doctors want medicare to work, but they feel alienated when they deal with the provincial governments which so often unilaterally take a position and set a fee schedule. When they turn to the federal Government and listen to the speeches from the NDP and Liberal members, they find that they are attacked in their personal and medical qualities. It is simply unacceptable for us in public life to be going after a very critical and important part of the medical profession in particular and the whole area of health care.
I personally believe that we should be listening, understanding and accepting that broad central opinion of the medical profession and that we should listen to them, because their true position is much different from what the NDP members are saying in their vicious personal attack on doctors. Having served on a hospital board, I happen to believe that doctors are absolutely critical to the successful operation of the whole system. I am also convinced that the average Canadian holds their doctor in high esteem and for very good reasons.
While they still have the highest average income-which is another reason why the doctors must understand the perceptions of others-they are still the hardest working people in this country. A 65 to 70-hour work week is still typical. I think the NDP have particular difficulty understanding the position of a professional person, especially doctors. They are never away from their practice. Their mind is never away from the concerns of a particular patient who is critically ill in hospital. That is one of the obligations of being a professional and the vast majority of doctors meet those obligations well.
When they say to me that they believe, particularly in the long run, that the system is underfunded, I believe that they are right. They are saying that if we continue with this closed, inflexible system that we have now, we cannot fund it over the long run. As our population becomes older, unless there is more flexibility and creativity in the system, it simply will not operate. The system will come tumbling down and we will have left our children and grandchildren in a much worse position than we are in. That is what the doctors are saying when they say that the system is underfunded.

I saw some statistics on the comparison of high technology equipment between Montana, which is one of the poorest states in the U.S., and my own Province of Alberta, which is one of the richest provinces in this country. The amount of high-tech equipment in Montana is unbelievable. It far exceeds what exists in Alberta. When one asks why we do not have that amount of equipment, the reason is that a system has been put in place which is inflexible and we have a federal Government that is unilaterally trying to dictate so many things rather than negotiating with the provinces. For instance, it does not recognize Alberta's unique situation and try to work something out, or work something out with New Brunswick, for example. We must have co-operation. Surely that is the lesson we must learn. Politicians should not try to politicize the issue as the Minister initially did. If she has learned nothing else out of this, I hope she has learned that.
Eighty-five per cent of the overall health care costs go to the hospital system, both in the operating costs of the hospital to cover nurses, nurses-aides and the equipment they use, as well as the capital equipment in the hospitals. This includes the "cat" scanners that we so desperately need and the high technology equipment we need to keep babies and senior citizens alive.
I believe the doctors when they say that the current system and the tensions have caused many medical people, in certain specialties particularly, to emigrate to the United States. I suggest it is mostly cardiac surgeons and ophthalmologists who leave. Those doctors leave not only for the money; it is also a matter of equipment and a matter of attitude. They leave because they do not believe that the existing inflexible system will offer any reasonable solution in the near future.
To my mind the exodus of doctors is serious. In 1981 a total of 1,050, if you include interns, resident physicians and civilian physicians, left the country. In 1982 some 1,196 medical people left. That is a serious drain of high professional skills.
The doctors in my home city of Lethbridge, who serve some 120,000 people in all, tell me that it is certain categories of specialists who are going. Under the medical fee schedule, for an operation for which they will receive some $500, or even $900 if they extra-bill another $400, for that same operation Montana pays $3,000. While money is partly the reason they leave, I believe doctors when they tell me another reason they leave is their attitude, that they do not see any hope here.
The United States will not disappear. We must have a system which will allow doctors to stay here and feel comfortable here. It is true that certain steps can be taken in the Province of Quebec in terms of permitting them to opt out and imposing a system where neither the doctor nor the patient can collect the medicare fee. However, this cannot be done in the rest of the country because many of the doctors in Quebec are trapped, in a sense, because they want to work within their own language and culture. The doctors in the rest of the country are not so confined and they will leave. The people who will suffer will be our daughters, sons and grandchildren.
I believe doctors when they say that this rapidly aging population will totally inundate the system. I believe them when they say that we need to have more long-term care. As
Canada Health Act
they point out, often some 30 per cent of the acute hospital beds are filled with long-term patients. If those people could be moved into long-term units, it would free 30 per cent of the beds which would then allow people to be moved through the acute hospital system more quickly and eliminate the long line-ups which worry the doctors so much. People will not be dying in their homes because they cannot get into hospital.
The system is underfunded because it has been so inflexible. The long-term auxiliary hospitals and the chronic care hospitals, which cost approximately $40 or $50 per day per bed compared with the $350 a day in the acute hospital system, cannot be put into place. Surely if more money were put into that it would be an investment that would pay off for all of us.
There is no doubt that the doctors themselves can and indeed must do more. They also have an extreme group among them which says that this issue is a question of freedom and individual rights. While we all have those rights, the vast majority of doctors are prepared to work within the system, but what they must do with respect to the extra fees is to get the medical profession together and reorganize their own schedule. The doctors do not seem to object to certain specialists extra-billing, so they must believe that the service is worth the extra money. In that case, they should be changing their own schedule and offering a higher amount of money for that particular service.
The doctors can do a lot more for themselves and I hope they will undertake to do so. I realize that it is a complicated process to change that schedule but there are in existence relative values for surgical and medical procedures. Their present fee schedules do not reflect those relative values and the medical profession could get that under control.
They must sit down and simply negotiate a better process with the provincial governments. As a result of this process I hope that the provincial governments will be more flexible with their doctors. One of the reasons the doctors will not give up this privilege or right, as they say, of extra billing is that they do not trust politicians. They have good reason not to trust politicians because politicians at the provincial level have frequently taken unilateral action and simply imposed fee schedules. This does not give the doctors reason to believe that their case has even been heard, let alone sympathetically heard and rejected. It is one thing to have negotiations and lose those negotiations. Why use a false argument to get out of changing this? Why does the Government not just say that it has less money so will transfer less money because it needs it for national purposes? Why does it not act honestly? The provinces would probably

agree to that, rather than have the gimmick of cancelling the revenue guarantee that had been lost five years ago.

Mr. Speaker, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall looked into the whole question of whether the federal transfers of money to the provinces were spent on that. He found that the money was all spent. Canada Health Act
there are procedures which we cannot take in this country now, Mr. Speaker. We must send our people down to the United States. That is the dangerous part of this problem. Mr. Speaker,
I am very pleased this afternoon to participate in the second reading stage of Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act. I have been very interested in this general field for a great number of years. When I first ran for Parliament back in 1968, an issue in that campaign was whether the recently passed new Medical Care Act would actually be proclaimed and, of course, it was proclaimed by the Liberal Government later that year.
I was also one of the seven Members of Parliament from all three Parties who took part in the fiscal arrangements task force under the chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) which held hearings all around Canada in 1981 on the then status of medicare and some other matters which were jointly funded by the federal and provincial governments. In addition, for the last year I have been the Chairman of the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs and I hope to be re-elected as its Chairman when the Committee is reorganized within the next few days. This Bill, of course, will come before our standing Committee for further study once the second reading stage is completed.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that all Hon. Members will work toward the strengthening of medicare, which is one of Canada's greatest social policy achievements and, for the people of Canada, the single most popular Government program. Over the years, the principles of medicare have become an important fibre of our social system. Access to good health care is not just a privilege enjoyed by those who can afford it. It is the right of everyone in Canada. Although few Canadians alone can afford to pay the real costs of health care, as a society working together we can afford to do so. We do not tax the sick. We share the burden and prepay our health insurance to buy peace of mind.
The medicare program is based on the principle that necessary hospital and medical services be accessible to all residents of Canada regardless of their financial circumstances. Thus, medicare means to the elderly, who have contributed so much to Canada, that they will be cared for. It means that the ordinary citizen will not be ruined by unexpected and sometimes staggering medical bills and that children will not have to suffer because their parents are unable to pay. Canadians know that universal medicare is more than an ideal. It is a practical and efficient program, and one which is worth preserving.
All sectors involved benefit from medicare. The patient is freed from the extra burden of health spending when the trauma of illness alone weighs so heavily. Physicians are assured of payment for their services while retaining professional freedom, and hospitals have more financial security and can better serve all Canadians. What has become evident,

January 20, 1984
Canada Health Act
however, is that through the practices of extra billing by physicians and the charging of user fees by hospitals, the principles of medicare are being undermined.
Concern about the phenomena of opting out and extra billing, about user fees and the level of services provided in our hospitals, is high. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) spoke in the House on this subject just last Monday. The doubling of extra charges from $50 million since 1978 to over $100 million in December, 1983, which she illustrated, draws attention to the fact that extra billing is a growing problem. Extra billing imposes a financial barrier to access to health care. Studies show, as we all know, that the poor, the elderly and those with large families are deterred by user charges and extra billing. User charges and extra billing undermine the basic principle that the cost of medically necessary health care should be borne by society so that people are not financially penalized for being sick.
Both the Breau task force and the report of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall underline the threat to medicare which these practices pose. In his report in 1980, Mr. Justice Hall stated the following at page 27:
If extra billing is permitted as a right and practised by physicians in their sole discretion, it will, over the years, destroy the program, creating in that downward path the two-tier system incompatible with the societal level which Canadians have attained.
In the Breau task force report, the following statement of our committee can be found on page 110, and I quote:
The task force believes that doctors are a critical part of the health delivery system and should be well paid for their professional work and fully compensated for the expenses of their practices.
However, the task force feels that the legitimate interests of doctors must give way to the broad public perception that uncontrolled billing of patients beyond the levels of professional medical insurance plan schedules, will ultimately destroy Medicare.
Some supporters of the practice of charging user fees argue that abuses of the health care system are reduced by this method. This has been proven untrue. Our Committee and the Breau task force report stated at page 108, and I quote:
A number of studies have suggested that the application of effective user charges leads to an immediate reduction in the utilization of services by patients, that the impact selectively affects more adversely the economically disadvantaged, and that there is no evidence that it contributes to a reduction in "abuse" of the rights to services.
Abuse of the system is in fact somewhat of a red herring, Mr. Speaker, as it is the physician who ultimately decides who will be admitted to the hospital and who will not. Hopefully, only those in medical need are in fact being admitted now by physicians. Halting the growing erosion of the basic principles of medicare is a raison d'etre for the tabling of Bill C-3, and the Act will be effective in this. Discussion of issues relating to the health expenditures will, of course, surface in this debate, and the issue of underfunding has already arisen. However, I believe the facts are clear in this regard. Prior to 1977, the federal contributions we made were made on a cost-sharing basis, that is, approximately 50 per cent of provincial expenditures on hospital and medical care. The federal Government and most of the provinces felt that this was too inflexible and did not provide incentives for improving efficiency in provincial programs. The change from cost sharing to bloc funding was a mutual effort strongly supported by many provinces and seen as a step forward for all concerned. Since 1977, federal transfers for health care have been greater than they would have been if the old cost sharing had continued. In those six years the provinces have received a total of $3.2 billion more than they would have received under the former program. Federal contributions to the Provinces under Established Programs Financing for medicare over the past three years has been as follows: In 1981-82 fiscal year, $7.7 billion, an increase of 12 per cent from the previous year; in 1982-83, $8.7 billion, an increase of 12 per cent; and in 1983-84, the current fiscal year, $9.5 billion, an increase of 10 per cent. Increases such as these during the tight fiscal period we recently went through are symbolic of the commitment to health care that this Government holds. The health areas of the Established Programs Financing were one of the few exceptions to this Government's six and five restraint program.
Over the past decade, Mr. Speaker, health spending in Canada has fluctuated between 7 per cent and 8 per cent of our GNP. In 1982, it reached $30.1 billion or 8.4 per cent of the GNP allocated to the health sector. In that respect Canada is currently about average among OECD countries. It is significant to note that the Canadian health care system generates services of equivalent quality at lower unit costs, while also providing universal prepaid coverage and reasonable accessibility to basic health care for all residents. Thus the level of spending should be lower here than in the U.S. where, for example, high malpractice insurance, business costs to physicians and pricing practices all inflate the cost of service to U.S. citizens.
As a Government we are proud of the continuing success of medicare, but it is our intention to build in even more guarantees with the tabling of Bill C-3. The fundamental objective of this new Act is simply to preserve the basic principles of medicare. The existing Acts which define the principles and conditions underlying hospital and medical insurance are the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, and the Medical Care Act, which are 25 and 17 years old respectively. Recent developments have served to highlight how generally and vaguely some of the principles were defined, and there is a wide consensus that there should be a new Act.
Bill C-3 sets out the program criteria and conditions of payment for the cash portion of federal contributions to the provinces for insured health services, and payments to the provinces for extended health care services. The insured health services covered by this legislation are all necessary hospital services, physician services and surgical-dental services performed in a hospital. The extended health care services covered by this legislation are nursing home intermediate care, adult residential care, home care and ambulatory health care.
The criteria a provincial health program must meet to be eligible for the full cash portion of the contribution are based on the long-standing principles which have served as the
January 20, 1984

backbone of Canadian medicare since its inception. However, the criteria have been adapted to answer the problems facing medicare today. As everyone in this House knows, the criteria are as follows.
Public administration: the program must be administered by a public authority accountable to the provincial Government. Comprehensiveness: the program must cover all necessary hospital and medical services, and surgical-dental services rendered in hospitals. Universality: One hundred per cent of residents of a province must be entitled to insured health services. Portability: the waiting period for new residents must not exceed three months; insured health services must be made available to Canadians temporarily out of their own province, at no extra charge to patients; payment for services out of province must be paid by the home province at host province rates, and payment for services out of country are to be at the home province rate. Accessibility: reasonable access to insured health services is not to be precluded or impeded, either directly or indirectly, by charges or other mechanisms. Reasonable compensation must be made to physicians and dentists providing insured health services. Adequate payments must be made to hospitals in respect of insured heath service. The conditions of payment that the provinces must meet to be eligible for the full cash portion of the federal contribution and payment also include the provision of reasonable information on the operation of the program to be supplied by the provinces to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Federal contributions to the programs are to be given appropriate visibility.
In addition to these conditions, the Act also states that extra billing and user charges must not be permitted except as outlined in the regulations attached to this Act. Where a provincial plan fails to satisfy any one of the program's criteria, or the province fails to comply with either of the two conditions of payment, the Act provides that cash portion of the federal contribution or payment may be reduced. This is discretionary and must be preceded by consultation with the province. Where a province fails to comply with the condition of payment relating to extra billing and user charges, the Act provides for a non-discretionary reduction of the cash portion of the federal contribution by the amount charged to extra billing or user charges. For the first three years after proclamation, however, funds withheld from provinces because of extra billing or user charges will be held in the public accounts of Canada and shall be paid to the province if the practice of extra billing or user charges is eliminated during those three years.
Medicare, Mr. Speaker, is one of the great social achievements for Canadians, and this Act will solidify and clarify its basic principles to ensure that every Canadian, no matter the age or income level, will have the absolute right to necessary physician and hospital care.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think this issue has been fairly dealt with by either the Government or the Official Opposition. I know the Hon. Member is aware of the position put forward by the Canadian Nurses' Association which paid
Canada Health Act
attention to the fact that the federal Government delivered some of the funds he has talked about to a revamping of the way in which health care is delivered. There is, for example, the more effective use of health care professionals such as nurse practitioners, as mentioned by the Hon. Member for Hamilton West. Then there is health prevention, health education, and community health care clinics where professionals work as teams in delivering health care in the community. There are community-based health services to the chronically ill and elderly. However, the particular legislation before us today deals with none of that, and it is not likely it will be opened again for many years to come. Other speakers, both from your Party and from the Official Opposition, say that this is an effective method of delivering health care and is cost effective. Yet neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives are prepared to stand up and say that the Bill is deficient in that aspect, that it does not apply real funding so as to provide an incentive for that kind of programming.
Could you explain what your position is going to be when the Bill is before the House?
