speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly).

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this important debate which touches upon one of the most fundamental questions affecting Canadians. It touches on one of the most fundamental questions, but it does not begin adequately to deal with Canada's health care needs. When my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), spoke on this Bill at its introduction, he identified two major areas of concern for our Party. He said that he had very serious questions as to whether Bill C-3 had an adequate mechanism to do what it intends to do, that is, to prevent user fees and extra billing. We are very concerned that user fees and extra billing are only the symptoms of the disease and are not the underlying disease affecting medicare. I would like to deal with both of those areas of concern very briefly.
The New Democratic Party has consistently opposed user fees and extra billing. For four years we have heard the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill asking the Minister what she was going to do about this billing practice. In this sense the Bill is at least three and one half years late. The Hall report of September 1980 indicated that this practice should be stopped. We can fairly say that without the persistent efforts of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill and other members of our Party no action would have been taken on this matter at all. The Tories were very silent on this entire question of extra billing and user fees until the Bill was practically introduced.
Our Party has very serious questions as to whether or not the dollar for dollar penalties will in fact deter provinces from imposing user fees or allowing extra billing. People who support these practices claim that the Act is a useful deterent against the frivolous use of medical facilities or of doctors' time. No doubt there are a certain number of hypochondriacs in our society who do take up, in an inappropriate way, a great deal of medical attention. Perhaps this indicates that we need to think of a different system which can meet some of the needs of so-called hypochondriacs. They do have needs. Nobody in their right health, body and mind, is going to spend time sitting in a doctor's waiting room, at least no doctor's waiting room that I have ever seen. People who spend time unnecessarily on medical appointments have concerns that need to be addressed, which our present medical system does not do. If user fees and extra billing deter these people from using up doctors' time, even more than that they will deter poor and needy people from using medical facilities and from going to a doctor at a time when they need medical help.
It is important to remember that although user fees and extra billing may deter poor people from using these facilities, user fees and extra billing pay only a fraction of the total cost of medical care. This creates a very serious problem which the House should think about for a moment.
I would like to use a rather far out example which might put this in perspective. Imagine a province that had approximately one million adults in which the government decided that it would be a good idea to give every adult a new $1,000 TV set. This became the program. Then a new government came in and decided that somehow it was immoral to give people something for nothing. It decided that because the TV set program was very popular it did not want to do away with it entirely but it would impose a $100 cost for these $1,000 TV sets. Theoretically, with a million people that would mean that they would save $100 million. In fact, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case at all. Some people would not be able to afford the $100. For the poor people who could not afford to pay the $100 for the $1,000 TV set, the Government would save not $100, but $900. When poor people are excluded from the use of medicare facilities that are paid for out of public funds, Mr. Speaker, they are not getting their fair share. This is one of the basic concerns that we have. Theoretically, a province could suffer the dollar for dollar penalties that are imposed by Bill C-3 but could still come out ahead of the game because there would be a decreased use of facilities by people who could not afford to pay those user fees.
In our Party we are concerned about medicare premiums. Last year in British Columbia premiums accounted for some $315 million. The Minister herself spoke about medicare premiums and pointed out how unfair and inefficient they were. Our Party and I would like to know what this Bill and the regulations attached to this Bill do with respect to medicare premiums. What relationship is there between the 100 per cent universality requirement of the Bill and the payment of premiums? Who defines what constitutes 100 per cent coverage? There are a lot of questions about that and I suspect that the Government does not really have adequate answers. We are concerned that the disincentives, the dollar for dollar penalty, will not really meet the objectives that the Government has set for it. On top of that, there are absolutely no incentives for positive action. There are no incentives for provinces which have never allowed extra billing or provinces which have never collected premiums or imposed user fees or for provinces that act expeditiously to do away with them. We believe that perhaps you can catch more flies with honey than with vinegar and some positive incentives might help.
Our second major area of concern is that dealing with user fees and extra billing really deals with the symptoms. The proposed Canada Health Act leaves us locked into a very expensive health care model. It offers no financial help to make that model run. I would like to use my own Province of British Columbia as an example. I do so noting that I am in no way an apologist for the present British Columbia Government. That Government has very badly mismanaged the
January 20, 1984

economy. In a mean-spirited way it has introduced cutbacks in education and social service. In a very shortsighted way that Government has cut back vital programs in forestry and so on. But in health care British Columbians, on top of provincial mismanagement, have to carry the burden of federal underfunding.
Last week when I was in my riding I met with a wide variety of health care workers, doctors, nurses, hospital administrators, board members, orderlies and cleaning staff. They showed a great deal of concern about what was going to happen to the medical situation in British Columbia. They told me that floors in some hospitals had been shut down. I heard of one long-term care situation. Fortunately, it was not within my riding. On night shift one nurse and one aide were responsible for 75 patients, some of whom were incontinent and some who needed a lot of help and care, others had difficulty eating. The aides did not have time to feed them normal food and so all the food was put through the blender. This is the ghetto to which we have relegated some of these people. Acute care beds are being used for chronic care patients because the cost of maintaining chronic care is lower than that for acute care patients. Elective surgery is postponed and postponed again. In an increasing number of cases it is postponed until surgery becomes critical. Doctors in British Columbia got a fair amount of publicity last year when they postponed part of a very handsome salary increase. At the same time hospital employees had a new contract which leaves them far behind the current rate of inflation. Even though the Government boasts about how low it has brought inflation, the new contract leaves these workers far behind.
When I talked to people on hospital boards they estimated that 6 per cent to 10 per cent of revenue came from user fees. They had absolutely no confidence that the Socred Government would make up any increased deficit. They said there was no more fat in the system. There had already been cut-backs and any further cut-backs in financing would mean an increasing deterioration in patient care. This is the situation facing medical care in British Columbia. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the Government on behalf of the people of British Columbia, that all of this federal-provincial squabbling about who is going to pay the next dollar is obscene. While that is happening, our medical care system is being eroded. The federal Government does not provide adequate funding for the present model, and it gives absolutely no incentive to develop other new and more cost efficient models.
There has been a fair amount of reference to the Canadian Nurses Association's submission about the increased use of nurses. I would like to refer to page 73 of the Hall report. It mentions a number of pilot studies that have been made about the use of nurses. One of these studies done by the Victorian Order of Nurses had a nurse attached to a team of five family physisians. Let me quote:
This study showed that, generally, patients preferred the nurse for many health care services and this preference increased with the amount of care given; that length of hospital stays also could be shortened, particularly for surgical procedures and for psychiatric disorders, because discharge planning and follow-
Canada Health Act
up care were available; and that hospital admissions of terminally-ill and dying patients could be reduced when the family wished it.
It is not, as the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) suggest, that there are no studies and we do not know how patients respond. Patients have responded very positively. There can be a greater use of nurses precisely in such areas as health promotion and sickness prevention, as well as at the other end of the health care spectrum in terms of functional support of people who have chronic illnesses. We do not provide support for those until they have been allowed to degenerate into some kind of situation where acute care is once again warranted. They are then returned to an acute care situation. When that situation improves slightly, they are put out again with no kind of ongoing support. This is the area when nurses can be a great deal of help. This will be cost effective and it is something the Bill should be addressing.
In addition to expanding the possibilities for health care by professionals, I believe we need a more holistic approach to health than the present medicare system recognizes. There is a law of diminishing returns in the use of medical expertise and equipment. Perhaps the Indian people of Canada can be a good example here. Not all health problems can be solved by having more doctors and bigger and better equipped hospitals. For example, in the West Coast community of Bella Bella, a Doctor George Darby went there as a medical missionary at the beginning of this century. When he retired in the 1950s some of the Indian people in Bella Bella said to him, "Before you came, our babies all died. Now they all live". That is very moving testimony. But then something terrible happened. In the late 1960s and 1970s there was a rash of suicides among young people in Bella Bella. This situation was not limited to Bella Bella; it was a phenomenon which took place in many Indian communities across Canada. Some of the very lives which Doctor Darby had saved as babies, some of the most sensitive and talented, committed suicide. Others died in boating accidents and some became victims of the city. No matter how modern the hospital at Bella Bella or how many doctors and how well trained they might be, they cannot meet this kind of problem. Mr. Justice Tom Berger put his finger on this problem when he quoted from a Health and Welfare document in his report on Indian and Inuit health consultation. Let me quote:
It has become apparent that government's efforts to improve the health of Indian people are no longer having the desired effect. Our standard medical tools do not seem to address the problems of high hospitalization rates, violence, anti-social behaviour, suicide-all indices of an accelerating crisis of health and social breakdown. We always thought that, as health professionals, we knew what Indians needed with respect to health care, and in areas where we concentrated our attention, such as communicable diseases and maternal and child health, we began to see improvements in health status.
In other areas they were completely helpless. The conclusion which Mr. Justice Berger and our own Indian Self-Government Committee reached is that Indian people have to have control over their own lives and communities.
I would like to share with the House a story about an Indian family which was summarized by Richard Cleroux in an

January 20, 1984
Canada Health Act
article in the January 12 edition of The Globe and Mail. Birdie and Joyce Cantin and their three daughters lived in the Wabigoon Reserve in northwestern Ontario. They had a modest home with reasonable furniture. She had a job and he picked up part-time work. About a year ago the three daughters began developing a series of illness-the flu, an ear infection, an eye infection, impetigo, skin rashes, blabber infections, chest infections and abdominal pains. The local health nurse investigated and discovered that the sewage system had backed up inside the house. There was raw sewage in the crawl space. The entire house and all their goods had been contaminated. The house was condemned and the band council was told to find a new house for the Cantin family. Of course the band council could not do that because, like all band councils across Canada, it had no more housing money; in fact it was $80,000 in the hole.
Last December the Cantin family moved to Winnipeg. From being an independent family on the Wabigoon Reserve, it became a welfare family in Winnipeg. Because they are now living off the reserve, it seems that the federal Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has very little concern about them. They have no work and they are demoralized.
I would like to read the last paragraph of Richard Cleroux's article. It says:
Joyce no longer has her job. Birdie is having trouble finding work. He's unskilled, has no credentials and has never worked in the city. They live off welfare. They get $148 a week. They moved into a City of Winnipeg public housing unit on the outskirts of the city. The rent is only $195 a month. They pay it out of their welfare money.
There's not much to do where they are. Joyce goes to bingoes a lot. And Birdie sits at home minding the girls. The girls love the city. They are at school. They watch television and draw beautiful pictures of skyscrapers and can hardly wait to get into the pinball arcades.
I talked with the mother on the telephone this week. She fears the family is headed for skid row. This is one health problem with which we are not dealing. There are other similar health problems. We in the NDP are concerned about environment health. It is something on which we would like to see the Government take action. For example, there is the situation in Key Lake arising out of the use of wood preservatives by woodworkers in British Columbia.
I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion,
I say that we are concerned about the mechanisms for dealing with user fees and extra billing. They are not adequate. Bill C-3 falls short of what the health care system needs, to be up to date in the 1980s.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. Was the Hon. Member differentiating between nurse practitioners and nurses? Certainly his comments about nurses are not denied by anyone in the medical field. They are traditional support for doctors. They work in operating rooms and they provide at home care. They make rounds with various organizations such as the Victorian Order of Nurses and the St. Elizabeth Order of Nurses. It has never been and will not be disputed that they are an integral part of medicine.
When one talks about nurse practitioners, one has to take a different approach. It is a good, sound approach. It is something new that is being developed. At the moment it works best in clinics. The Hon. Member talked about what he has read. I can tell him what is happening in areas such as Hamilton where the program has been given a good trial. Working in clinics, nurse practitioners carry a great deal of the burden of the work of doctors. They work with them. However, when the Hon. Member talks about nurse practitioners being initial medical care providers, it must be noted that this is a new field which is being developed. It has great merits, but it has to be sold to the public. In due course it will find a rightful place in the Canadian health care system.
Did the Hon. Member draw that distinction or have that distinction in mind when he made comments concerning the contributions of nurses to the medical health care system?

Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for Hamilton West for his question. I frankly admit that I am not well versed in the distinction, but I would like to refer to page 73 of the Hall report which referred to the Beaverton project that included nurse practitioners. I would like to read the following summary contained in the report of the Hall Commission:
In the "Beaverton Project", another Canadian demonstration project, the practice setting extended over an area of approximately 85 square miles with a large proportion of the population (26 per cent) over 65 years of age. One objective of the project was to demonstrate that a qualified nurse practitioner could operate as co-practitioner taking primary responsibility for significant office load, thus allowing the physician to devote more time to the management of complex medical problems of his patients.
It referred to the practitioner working within the office and continued:
With a high level of independent decision-making the nurse fulfilled the functions of providing primary health care, of intervention in episodic incidents or occurrences, of monitoring chronic care, and of promoting and maintaining health. The investigation concluded that home visiting by the nurse practitioner decreased the need for hospital or other institutional care; she also was able to identify early health problems which had they been left unattended might have led to more serious health problems and eventually to more health care costs.
The Beaverton project referred to practitioners operating in an office-clinic setting and home visits and suggested that both cases were helpful.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the comments of the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands on the matter of providing a more full role for the nursing profession within the medicare system.
I believe that in his concluding remarks he touched on a slightly different topic. He wanted to address more fully some of the problems relating to occupational health, particularly with regard to the problems faced by people in the plywood industry in British Columbia and elsewhere. Would he expand on those remarks? In my constituency of Kootenay West there are many people who are vitally interested and would appreciate his comments.

January 20, 1984

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that question because 1 did not have time to expand on it. A study was conducted of woodworkers in Port Alberni two years ago. These workers had infrequent or frequent and daily exposure to polychloro-phenols used in wood preservatives on the West Coast. The study found that there was a high incident of respiratory problems, nervous disorders, skin ailments and cancer.
In the last few weeks I was pleased to see that a $15,000 grant was made by the Department of National Health and Welfare for a further study of the problem as it relates to mortality from cancer. It is my belief-and certainly it is on record by the International Woodworkers of America-that the use of such preservatives should be banned until they can be proven safe. If there is a study going on right now about the relationship between the use of these products and cancer, and if other studies have indicated a high correlation in the complaints, there should certainly be a moratorium imposed on the products until they have been declared safe.
In connection with the whole question of health and safety, I urge Hon. Members to look at the last issue of Goodwin's Magazine which contains a very graphic story of death from asbestos. One part of it is about a worker in Whitby, Ontario employed by the Johns-Manville Corporation. That company showed a completely callous disregard not only for his health while he was working there, but also for his needs when he became sick. It is incumbent upon the Government now to bring in revisions to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code dealing with occupational health and safety. Three Ministers in this House have dealt with the question and we still have not seen the revisions. They are important to every Canadian worker and his family.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to speak for a few moments on Bill C-3, the alleged new Canada Health Act. It does not bring very much that is new and futuristic. It could be more properly styled simply a Canadian contribution to the provinces for insured services.
I was rather surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley) say that only 80 per cent of his constituents replied to a questionnaire stating that they favoured a publicly-funded medicare program. One could hardly find a person on the street who does not favour a publicly-funded medicare program, a program so essential to the well-being of Canadians.
In introducing this Bill, the Minister said that she was proud of our medicare program, meaning our existing medicare program. She said it was one of the best, if not the best, universal, top quality prepaid health care system in the world.
This Party, the Progressive Conservative Party, has made a substantial commitment over the years to health care which makes it possible for today's Minister to make such a statement. Indeed, Mr. T. C. Douglas said of a fellow colleague from Saskatchewan, "If it had not been for the co-operative negotiations of the Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker with the
Canada Health Act
provinces, Canada may not have achieved medicare as we know it today". He was one of the more objective, constructive NDP-CCF members.
I emphasize the co-operative negotiations that led to the implementation of the Hospital and Diagnostic Services Act, so different from the approach and single-mindedness of the several Liberal Governments as they were confronted with the problems and issues in the evolution of medicare.
The present Minister has learned her heavy-handed and confrontational approach well. In 1969 when the Province of Ontario was coerced into the national plan, the then Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro), said: "Comply or you will fail to qualify for federal contributions". Where have we heard those words before? That was at a time when the national plan was practically funded by Ontario taxpayers.
It was stated then, as it is still being stated, that the federal position is not one of a medicare plan per se. It is simply a financial proposal under which the federal government will meet a portion of the cost borne by the provinces. The provinces are responsible for the introduction, implementation, administration and operation of the medicare plan. Let us come back to the best health plan in the world. If there is any argument at all, it is based on the cost of the system, the cost of the plan and how it should be met.
Provincial Treasuries are strapped. Instead of the co-operative negotiations of John Diefenbaker with the provinces, we have a Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and a Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) holding back on the established transfers to the provinces, transfers of funds to which they are entitled. They are reluctantly handed over as though they were alms for the poor.
The Minister of Finance said: "It is significant that federal aid to the provinces is increasing at a time when federal resources are under considerable strain". I wonder how much they know about the problems of the provincial Treasuries. Is this the kind of rhetoric that builds trust and confidence between levels of government regarding a program such as medicare, which has the support of practically all Canadians of all political stripes, without regard to economic conditions or circumstances? The answer to supporting and enhancing medicare lies in co-operative negotiation between the provinces and the federal government, the means by which we used to resolve federal and provincial problems in days gone by. Against that, this Government's approach has been an "us" against "them" approach.
The Minister says: "I will talk. I am prepared to negotiate, but I won't compromise. Don't tell me about the complex problems of medicare". This is more than simply regrettable. It is an outright abdication of the federal Government's responsibilities to medicare. I would like to take a moment to illustrate that fact.
For many reasons the public has come to regard the medicare debate as one revolving around extra billing, user fees- goodness knows, we have heard a lot about that in this

January 20, 1984
Constitution Act, 1867
debate-and health insurance premiums to a lesser extent. Each is said to be bad. These are simply symptoms of a problem which goes much deeper. Extra billing and user fees are, for the most part, functions of underfunding. If anyone here does not know and believe that there is underfunding in the delivery of medicare service today, they are not acquainted with the position of the medicare world.
Canadians want and expect the best care system available. To provide that system requires large sums of money and close co-operation between all levels of government. We need some consensus as to the base level of medicare, what is desirable and what is affordable. What can Canadians afford to pay?
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might call it four o'clock?

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 REQUEST TO CHANGE BOUNDARIES OF NATIONAL CAPITAL

speechtext:
Mr. Gaston Isabelle (Hull), seconded by Mr. Turner, moved that Bill C-206, an Act to Amend the Constitution Act of 1867 (national capital of Canada) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
January 20, 1984

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill, which is very straightforward, is to amend Section 16 of the Constitution Act of 1867, which reads as follows:
Until the Queen otherwise directs, the Seat of Government of Canada shall be Ottawa.
As I said at the beginning, the national capital area would be designated as the national capital of Canada. There are various reasons for this, Mr. Speaker, because if we refer to the history of the national capital area, we see that since the small village of Bytown was selected by the Queen in 1858, it was then ridiculed and called a forest centre and and a logging capital, the City of Ottawa as such has constantly developed.
The reason why I am asking for that amendment is that since the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden and even the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, we have always wanted to make of the capital of Canada a national symbol, the seat of our national languages or, if you prefer, the beating heart of our nation.
Up to now, I think that we have always thought of the capital of Canada as a city in Ontario. I have nothing against Ontario or Ottawa, but throughout the years, we have asked the Federal Government to contribute to the beautification of the region and we have been saying that it should not be restricted to the city of Ottawa. Parliament has continued to expand the region on the Quebec side, in the Outaouais region, and we are now saying that the National Capital Region is a product of Canadian federalism and reflects many of the familiar political, social, linguistic and cultural differences and ambiguities of Canadian society. It is typical of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the people who come to visit the Canadian capital simply visit an Ontario city, and I remember quite clearly that the former mayor Lorry Greenberg did not want Ottawa to share the honor of being the capital city with any other municipality in the National Capital Region. Now that Ottawa is bigger and that an Act passed in 1956 designates the neighbouring municipalities both in Ontario and in Quebec as part of the National Capital Region, I do not see why this region could not become officially the capital of Canada. Of course, this would take nothing away from Ottawa, which would keep its title of capital city, but at least, it would not be alone and would be part of the national capital, and the same would be true for Nepean, Gloucester, Vanier, Aylmer, Gatineau and Hull, because I am sure that such a capital would be a much more appropriate symbol than the city of Ottawa. Indeed, at a constitutional conference held in February 1969 in Toronto, it was even agreed that the cities of Ottawa and Hull and the surrounding areas constituted the National Capital Region.
If the cities so designated constitute a region known as the Canadian capital, I do not see why they should not be called the Capital of Canada. I can think of many politicians-I am
Constitution Act, 1867
not blaming them; they are quite justified-the Ontario Premier, for instance who, every time he comes to Ottawa, he always says how happy he is to be in the capital of Canada, Ottawa, Ontario, and he places much more emphasis on the fact that Ottawa is in Ontario than on the fact that it is the national capital. I am sure that there has been a lot of progress since 1896. Sir Wilfrid Laurier wanted to make Ottawa the Washington of the North. The Hon. Robert Borden also wanted to do the same when he created the Ottawa Improvement Commission, because the municipality did not have the facilities required to maintain the Canadian capital properly. I am sure that, with this change, the capital of Canada could reflect the various ethnic groups as well as the biculturalism and bilingualism that our capital should represent as the heart of the whole country.
I am sure that my colleagues who live in this region can appreciate these remarks more readily than many others who come to Ottawa for a few days or a few years. They do not share the same enthusiasm as the residents of the National Capital Region for whom the National Capital is the birthplace of the nation, so to speak, and it should represent everything Canada has to offer. It is a microcosm, a sort of mirror, a reflection of Canada.
That is the purpose of the message I wanted to convey, because although the region includes many municipalities, it can be said that the federal Government has never been quite at home in Ottawa, in the sense that it has always been subject to the laws of Ontario and the by-laws of the municipalities, and it has to spend money if it wants to improve the environment.
From 1947 to 1967, I think it spent $111 million to buy land, not to build but only to upgrade the Capital of Canada. If I may put it this way, it was the only way it could control the land over which it had no jurisdiction. By purchasing land through the National Capital Commission, the federal Government gained direct control over that land. It stands to reason that, had the National Capital Commission been unable to buy land, chances are the Parliament Buildings would not be where they are now. Because the federal Government, through its agencies, has no authority when it comes to building height regulations, and I am sure that if the federal Government had not acted as I said earlier in my remarks, that is built up a land bank to restrict construction, we would hardly be able to see the Parliament Buildings. As I keep saying, not only is the Capital the seat of Government, but it is also the soul and the fount of strength of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, those are the reasons why the National Capital Region should become the Capital of Canada. If it were, the municipalities which are part and parcel of the National Capital Region would be a lot less reluctant to co-operate than they have been for a number of years.
We have created various organizations on both sides of the river, they have multiplied and so overloaded the administra-

January 20, 1984
Constitution Act, 1867
tion that we now have the most overgoverned and indeed the most overtaxed region of Canada.
Whenever we have asked for the co-operation of the various regional governments, it has always been hard to get. This is why over the years I have always advocated a federal district, in order that the federal Government be at home here. But this is not for tomorrow, because we know what came out of the so-called co-operation between the various levels of government, both local and provincial.
I feel therefore, the time has come for something to be done along those lines. For sure, this will not bring in the slightest change in the current administrative structures; if anything, it will give some sense of pride to the people of the National Capital area who do not happen to live in the City of Ottawa proper, either side of the river and I am sure that once this is done, it will be much easier to set milestones along the road to whatever we should have had for years, even since 1857, that is a federal district. If I refer to a federal district it is because I think Queen Victoria, when she decided to designate Ottawa as the capital of Canada, Bytown as it was then called, may not have taken a good look at our geography, since as we know, in earlier times Canada's capital had changed places-Kingston, Montreal, Quebec, Toronto-before settling for Ottawa under Order-in-Council, by authority of the Queen, between Upper and Lower Canada. For this reason, a neutral area should have been selected, comprising a part of Lower Canada and a part of Upper Canada, to be the seat of the Government. Indeed, Section 16 of the Constitution does not refer to the Capital of Canada, but rather to the Seat of the Government of Canada. A seat can be moved, it can be expanded, it can be amended any way one likes. For that reason, I feel that the willingness of the House of Commons to amend Section 16 of the Constitution would enhance the pride of Canadians and provide a much larger dimension, a better image of what Canada actually is, because if there is one place in Canada that is ideally suited for a National Capital, it is the Ottawa-Hull area.
To those who suggest that an extraordinary process is required for amending Section 16, I say all that is needed is an Order-in-Council, simply adding Hull and the surrounding municipalities on both sides of the river, so that Canada's National Capital truly reflects the daily life of every Canadian. Because certainly visitors, whether they come from British Columbia or from New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island, are not particularly enthralled when coming to Ottawa to visit just another Ontario City.
Let there be no misunderstanding: I am not suggesting that we should get rid of Ottawa as such, but that we should make Ottawa part of the national capital region just as all the other municipalities which are now part of the national capital region. And I am sure that members of the House are aware of this major problem of a capital for a young country such as Canada, for we have had a flag for some twenty years and we
have a practically new, at least freshly patriated Constitution. In my opinion, what really matters now is to endow ourselves with a capital which clearly reflects the wills, aspirations and modus vivendi of all Canadians. It should occupy a neutral ground, outside the territory of any individual province, and I just cannot understand how a province such as Ontario can logically have two capitals. If there is disunity, if the West feels alienated, it may be because we have no meeting point where we could all get together and feel at home as Canadians. People from Western Canada think that they are away visiting Eastern Canada when they come to this Ontario city, and those from Eastern Canada think they have gone West when they are in the same Ontario city. Therefore, to dispel any doubt and give Canada a new image or impetus, in line with the novelties we have known over the past few years, including the flag, I think it is a matter of individual self-esteem and national pride to have a capital which reflects the character of all Canadians from coast to coast. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. [English]

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 REQUEST TO CHANGE BOUNDARIES OF NATIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) for bringing his proposal forward once again and I should like to make a few comments on it. It seems to me to be a practical idea and I have nothing against it. I must admit that many years before I came to this place, in the Parliament of Canada of 1965 and 1966, as I recollect, there was a small committee of Canadians set up who referred to themselves as the Riel Committee. It wanted Ottawa and the surrounding area to be taken out of the Province of Ontario and the Hull and Gatineau area taken out of the Province of Quebec, and something like an eleventh province set up, a truly different area apart from Quebec or Ontario which would be the capital territory as they have in Washington, D.C. or in Canberra, Australia. Quite frankly, I see a lot of merit in that idea. I rather like it, even though part of my constituency would fall into that new area and part of it would fall outside.
I feel there is a lot to commend that idea. I have not thought in great detail about this. I am sure there would be many complications and problems which would have to be worked out. However, I do know that in other parts of Canada, people really do not like to write to Ottawa, Ontario, when they are writing to the capital of the country. People out west do not think the capital should be Ottawa, Ontario. It should be Ottawa, Canada. Perhaps it should be called "Ottawa, Outaouais", something other than Ottawa, Ontario. I do not believe these people like writing to a Department of the Government in Hull, Quebec. I believe they would like to write to Ottawa, Canada. This is a feeling I know people out west have, as well as some people in the east.
Why not create a jurisdiction, taking away a small portion of land from the Province of Quebec and from the Province of Ontario, and creating a truly independent capital region? Not, however, a region as they have had in Washington, D.C., where the voters are not allowed to have anything to say. In
January 20, 1984

fact, they did not even have a vote. They could not even elect a municipal council until a few years ago. I do not want it to be a dictatorship. I would like it to have proper municipal voting patterns, perhaps a provincial legislative body, and it would have the federal Parliament. The federal Parliament, then, thought the National Capital Commission and the National Capital Region, would be able to assist the new legislative body of a provincial nature in carrying out projects to beautify and enhance the capital of Canada for all Canadians.
I have not thought through all of those ideas and I am sure there are many people who would counter them with other suggestions. Perhaps the question would be, would the Province of Quebec willingly give up Hull, and perhaps Gatineau, Gatineau Park and Aylmer, and allow it to fall into a new jurisdiction? And would Ontario willingly give up Ottawa, Kanata and some of the rural areas to a new jurisdiction? There may be some people who would say that there is no way those provinces would give up that territory. One would immediately ask why they would not, and it might be because they want the power, the jurisdiction, legislation and tax base of those people who live in those areas.
Perhaps it would be appropriate to consider this, and 1 suggest that if a meaningful discussion was started, the federal Government, in order to set up this new jurisdiction, might offer, in payment to the Provinces of Quebec and Ontario, a proportionate amount of their provincial debts considering the number of people who would be taken out of the two provinces compared to the rest of the population, which would add up to a few hundreds of millions of dollars. That might be attractive to them. And those provincial debts should naturally fall to the new jurisdiction backed by the federal Government, because the provincial debt reflects the number of people-in the province, and if some of the people are taken away with the land, then I feel the new jurisdiction should assume some of the responsibility, because those provinces have incurred that debt by building highways, transmission lines, and so on.
Those are some of the ideas I have, and I feel that the suggestion I might be making here goes beyond what the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) has suggested in his Bill. On the other hand, I feel quite confident that perhaps he would have liked to go as far as I have in my suggestion but thought that going part way would be the best way to start the ball rolling. It seems odd, if one looks back in history, that it was as far back as 1899 that the Government of the time first set up the Ottawa Improvement Commission to beautify and to enhance the capital of Canada, or the seat of Government, as it might be more appropriately called. The Government of the day wanted to make the capital something special for the people. As time progressed, the name was changed and the new Government, around 1926-27, brought in a new group called the Federal District Commission. Of course, it was in 1958 that a new piece of legislation came along and the National Capital Region was prescribed in that legislation. It was legislation introduced by the Government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. So this is certainly not a completely
Constitution Act, 1867
new idea. It is not a partisan idea and I feel it is being discussed here today in a nonpartisan way.
It seems that we have never gone beyond the stage of discussion or beyond the stage of implementing half steps and half measures. Section 16 says that the seat of Government will be Ottawa. We have moved to the point where the National Capital Region encompasses a large portion of the Province of Ontario, including Fitzroy Harbour, Pakenham, Almonte and places like Orleans on the east, so it is not just the City of Ottawa anymore. The National Capital Region stretches farther than that. It also encompasses the other side of the river in the Province of Quebec, which I feel is only appropriate as it takes in a more proper balance of the two cultural groups which I suppose founded this country in the sense of a country called Canada being formed. They were the instigating partners. I believe that a new jurisdiction should cover those areas and those cultural groups, including the civil law in what is presently the Quebec portion and the common law in the Ontario portion. They could both be encompassed in a new jurisdiction or province or capital region, whatever the name might be.
I would like to believe it might even go farther. The Hon. Member for Hull, in introducing the Bill, may have been more wise than I. He has taken that intermediate step in suggesting that we would deal with the whole area as being the seat of Government and the capital of Canada. I have one problem as to whether it should be Ottawa-Hull. I would prefer that the name "Ottawa" be retained as it is a historical name, a Canadian name, it is named after Indians, whereas "Hull", quite frankly, was adopted from the name of a city on the east coast of England. Perhaps that name does not have the same sort of Canadian content that a name adopted from the name of original native people in this country would have.
It might be more appropriate for the Bill to not be read at this time and perhaps the subject matter referred to a committee. It would seem to me that that might be a way of giving it an opportunity to be taken up by a committee and looked at in all of its dimensions.
I am not sure if that suggestion commends itself to the Hon. Member who has introduced this Bill, or to other Hon. Members who might want to speak on it, at least for a short period of time. I do not want to take up too much time, but I believe there is much merit in this idea. I think it would help to reflect the duality of this country. As I say, I have a certain reservation about the name "Ottawa-Hull", but those are technicalities which people can work around in one way or another. I would like to see an independent jurisdiction set up which could work out the problems directly with the federal Government rather than having two provinces quarreling over jurisdiction and where the buildings would be.
I think it should be pointed out that this area has changed much. When Canada became a reality we had three buildings here on Parliament Hill, the Centre Block, the East Block and the West Block. Those buildings housed all Members of

January 20, 1984
Constitution Act, 1867
Parliament, all Senators and all civil servants in this country. Now we have Tunney's Pasture and Confederation Heights and a proliferation of government buildings throughout the Ottawa area. In the last 10 or 12 years we have seen a proliferation of buildings on the other side of the Ottawa River in what is presently the City of Hull, to reflect the capital on both sides of the river. In essence I think most people, whether they liked it at the time or not, accepted then and accept now that the capital of Canada is on both sides of the Ottawa River. Indeed, the federal Government pours in considerable money to beautify not just Ottawa but the National Capital Region which takes in portions of both provinces. I would certainly favour this matter going to committee to be considered even beyond the scope of the Bill, but if necessary I would even support the Bill.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 REQUEST TO CHANGE BOUNDARIES OF NATIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and support whatever action is necessary in order that the Bill may become a reality in some shape or form. Many of the visitors who come here from as far as British Columbia-and I know many have come from my own constituency as well as others-regard the National Capital Region, not just the City of Ottawa or the City of Hull, as the capital. They look around and see the work done, particularly by the National Capital Commission, and they have the feeling that the region is the capital and the whole area represents the country. What they have seen they feel to be one, and they also feel it to be quite good.
As one who was a resident of this area back in the early 1960s for a couple of years, I know that the improvements which have been made, largely through the NCC, have given to all of us who have come to know this area or to visit it, a feeling of some pride. No matter how distant we may be in our own homes from what is regarded as the political centre of the country, we do have some pride in it and feel as though there has been a good job done. I would also say, perhaps a little tongue in cheek, that even though the nation's capital may not always be in the mainstream, by following this suggestion at least we will put the mainstream in the national capital. That may not be a bad idea as well.
In listening to the remarks of the Hon. Member who just spoke, I find myself a little concerned, as desirable as though it may be, about attempting to remove areas from either the Province of Ontario or the Province of Quebec. It seems to me that it is perhaps typically Canadian to have a capital in which jurisdictional squabbles are ever present. We sometimes tend to be isolated enough without asking for even more departures from the norm.
In listening to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), I note that he expressed, perhaps not misgivings, but some thoughts as to the fact that many Canadians may not regard this as the centre of the country. That is not unique in the Canadian experience. In my own Province of British Columbia the capital was selected in a colony separate from the major part of the mainland and so we had to cross the water in order to get to our provincial capital. That was entirely within the Canadian experience.
As an aside, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I, along with many other Members of the House on Tuesday evening, attended the gala performance at the National Arts Centre in honour of the visit of the Premier of China. No one could have mistaken that performance as being anything else but Canadian. Perhaps I felt more distinctively Canadian then than I had felt for some time, if not ever. The fact we can put together that kind of performance on relatively short notice, the fact that, as has been alluded to previously, we have in recent years adopted a number of symbols, a new national anthem, a national flag, a constitution, a charter, about which many people across the country feel pride and which they consider to be not only an instrument but as a symbol of nationhood and a coming of age, makes it entirely appropriate that we should find some way of expressing the duality of our major founding cultures and the uniqueness of those things which make us Canadian. We should recognize that taking a segment from both sides of the river and calling it the capital seems good and proper and is welcome.
I would just say again that whatever course the Hon. Member for Hull may choose to take on this Bill, he has our general support. We hope that in the not too distant future his intent will become a reality. We welcome the proposal.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 REQUEST TO CHANGE BOUNDARIES OF NATIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have looked at and considered this Bill very carefully. It says:
It is hereby declared that the national capital of Canada and the seat of the federal government of Canada shall consist of the city of Ottawa, in the Province of Ontario, and of the city of Hull, in the Province of Quebec, and also of such surrounding area as prescribed from time to time by the Parliament of Canada.
That is the essence of this particular Bill. The explanatory note says:
The capital of a country should not simply be considered its seat of government but should symbolize its authority and unity, and should project to the world the repository of the nation's soul.
In other words, this amendment to the Constitution will authorize Parliament to legislate so as to include in the National Capital all areas now included in the National Capital Region.
It may surprise the Hon. Member who proposed this Bill, but I find he has a great poverty of thought. I am opposing this Bill on the grounds that it does not go nearly far enough. He is proposing to include the whole area and yet to leave it out. He is proposing a Bill that does not accomplish what should be accomplished. Had his Bill been properly framed, I would be the first Member in the House to support it fully.
We all know the difference in taxation between the Province of Quebec and the Province of Ontario. We all know there are many immense Government buildings in the City of Hull, and that city should certainly be part of the capital of Canada. No doubt about that. I can certainly agree with that, but the Bill does not go far enough. I suggest to the Hon. Member that he did not frame his Bill in the proper way. The national capital should have become the national capital including Hull and the surrounding area and including Ottawa and the surrounding area. That is the real capital of this country. He should have proposed that this Government make representation to the Government of Ontario and the Government of Quebec
January 20,1984

that they give up this territory in order that a national capital area be designated, an area with its own laws and taxation on the same basis on which the District of Columbia in Washington, D.C. operates. On that basis I could approve this Bill.
There is no question at all that Hull is part of the national capital. But it is improper to have taxation in Quebec which causes Quebeckers to buy their gasoline in Ontario. It is improper that English Canadians cannot live across the river in the Gatineau Hills because of the difficulties involved with school taxes and proper schools for their children. It is improper that Ottawa and Hull are not totally bilingual, as I suggest a national capital of this kind should be.
This Bill is improper. It should not be passed. It should be tossed back and the Government should be required to go much further in that respect. We do need a national capital region.
As anyone wandering the streets of Ottawa knows, we have the RCMP, the Ontario Provincial Police, the City of Ottawa Police, the City of Hull Police and the Quebec Police. Frankly, I find that offensive. One policeman is bad enough, but five policemen from different jurisdictions, all operating within basically the same area, is offensive. The City of Ottawa and the City of Hull should be part of this Bill. There should be an amalgamation to make it truly the national capital. That we do not have. This Bill is not going to help it at all. Taxation within the National Capital Region should be equalized so that the person who owns a house in Hull pays the same taxes as does a person in Ottawa. Regardless of which side of the river a person buys his gasoline, the cost should be identical. If he buys a meal in a restaurant, his taxes should be the same. In other words, there should be a jurisdiction for the national capital, an area which is truly the national capital, as opposed to what we now have. The beautification that has taken place on the Ottawa side of the river should be extended fully to the Hull side of the river. We would no longer have the jurisdictional disputes in which an Ottawa painter paints half of the bridge and a Quebec painter has to paint the other half. Those kinds of disputes do not lead to national unity. Those kinds of problems which we are faced with are ridiculous. In a sovereign nation, a country of this size which means so much to all of us, it is time we ended the solitude which exists between Ottawa and Hull.
The Member nods at me. He agrees with me. Then why did he not go that far? Why do we have this simple Mickey Bill which, if passed, would only mean that we would perpetuate mistakes that have been made in the past? Let us put this country together by taking Hull and Ottawa and making them into what could be a great national capital and district. If we did that, it would certainly solve the problem in this Bill of not including Hull. I am not prepared to go part of the way. I want to go all the way. I want to do something for this country which would make for unity in the country rather than the two solitudes that exist on either side of the river. This Bill does not really contribute to that, in my view. It is too simple.
Constitution Act, 1867
Perhaps it is a step, but it is an inadequate step. If only that step were taken, the real issue involved in the situation would not be addressed.
Queen's Park, Quebec City and the Members of this House of Commons could solve this problem and give us a national capital which could be the finest in the world. They could give us a unity in this particular area within the confines of the ghetto that Ottawa is now and the ghetto that Hull is now by putting them together and having one civic government for the whole area and one police force for the whole National Capital Region. I think possibly that could be done. I think we could get an agreement out of two provincial Governments which have a tendency to fight with each other. We could get an agreement with a constitutional amendment which could set up such a region. All we would have to do would be to offer lower taxes to the whole area so as to have the full support of the citizenry. As a matter of fact, I suspect the people of Ottawa would welcome this. No one likes to be charged with Quebec taxes when he lives in Ontario. No one in Quebec likes to work in Ottawa and realize that his taxation is substantially lower than that of somebody who lives on the other side of the river. No one likes the idea that, depending on what education and school he wants for his children, there is a substantial difference in where his residence is.
Because of those factors I feel the Bill is inadequate. It does not go nearly far enough. It does not really deal with the problem which is a unit of disunity in the country.
I said that I thought the Hon. Member displayed poverty of thought. Perhaps that is a little strong. I would say that his intentions were excellent and noble. However, as I mentioned initially, he just did not think through to what the real implications should be, what could happen in this country and what a contribution the proper Bill could make to the total unity of this country.
If we had a capital region we might name the city Sir John A. MacDonald. I suspect there might be some difficulty with that. However, I am sure that we could find a name and dispense with Hull, Quebec and Ottawa, Ontario. We could have a name that truly reflects the national will, the will of the nation as a whole, and that truly means something to Canadians. It is their capital.
We see busloads of schoolchildren arriving here from now until the end of June. All Members have visitors who come and who are awed by the Parliament buildings. The Parliament buildings happen to be on the Ottawa side. Should the people of Quebec not be able to feel exactly the same pride in these buildings? That territory belongs to all of Canada. It is not part of Ontario, and Hull is not part of Quebec; it is part of the national capital. That is the answer to the situation rather than a Mickey Mouse Bill which simply includes Hull to a certain extent. I do not care what you call it. How it is policed can be worked out. The administrative functions, I am sure, can be amicably agreed to by everyone over a period of time. Taxation within the region would be taxation within the region and it would no longer matter on which side of the river you lived.

January 20, 1984
Constitution Act, 1867
I would personally be delighted. I think the Gatineau is among the most beautiful country in all of North America. I cannot live there. I cannot afford to. It simply is not possible as opposed to living on this side of the river. To me that is very wrong. My children are grown up. But I know many people with children who would sooner live on the other side of the river but cannot. I was talking to a new Member from British Columbia who won a by-election last August and one of the things I told him and warned him about was attempting to live on the other side of the river in the Hull area. I pointed out to him some of the things I have pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, about taxation, about the differences in hours, about the differences in food costs, about differences in the wine, beer and liquor stores and the costs involved on both sides of the river. Much as he wanted to bring his French to the point where he would be absolutely and totally bilingual, he had to take a very good look at the situation before he realized there were penalties involved for him, that there were demerits, and that living over there would not work for him. Reluctantly, he lives in Ottawa. Frankly, that is a sad situation. It is unfair, and that is not a contribution to national unity. The Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) had a good idea, but he did not carry it far enough. I am not prepared to vote for such a simple Bill when so much more is needed. This country should take a very good look at the situation. Darn it, it is our national capital. It should be the National Capital Region. It should be a separate jurisdiction from what goes on in Queen's Park, Toronto or what goes on in Quebec City. The national capital should reflect the whole of the country.
In my view, the City of Ottawa and the City of Hull should both be part of the national capital for the very purposes of national unity. The Premier of British Columbia should have as much to say about what takes place in the National Capital Region as the Premier of Ontario does now or the Premier of Quebec. The Premier of Nova Scotia should have some words that he can express about what his feelings are on the National Capital Region, just as all Canadians should have something to say about it, whether they are French, English, Swedish, German, or what have you. If we want a truly national capital and if we want a truly National Capital Region, then this Bill is not the answer. We should have a much stronger, more vigorous Bill that will set up this area as the national capital of this country in the proper sense, in the same sense as the American genius who arrived at the concept of the City of Washington, D. C. and the District of Columbia, which is not subject to any of the individual states surrounding it. I do not think that is really such a far out idea. I do not think there would be much against that idea throughout the country. It would certainly equalize taxation on both sides of the river. It would mean the guy with the shoe store in Hull and the guy with the shoe store on the Sparks Street Mall would know they are being treated absolutely equally. In some of the areas there is great difficulty now, and I mention gasoline again. It is not difficult to see by going back and forth across the river, that gas prices are considerably higher in one area than in another
because of taxation. All one has to do is look at the provincial income taxes to realize there is an impediment on one side. That does not necessarily mean it is all bad in Quebec either. Quebec has some things that I would like to see here. It would mean that everyone living in the National Capital Region would be treated on exactly the same basis.
There is a great inequality now. Things will not change under a Mickey Mouse Bill like this. Things will only happen if we can get agreement that we can get a separate jurisdiction and if this particular area becomes, in the truest sense of the word, a real national capital. That is what I would like to see. That is the kind of Bill that I would be prepared to vote for, not this one. I say that with great respect, Sir. I understand the Hon. Member's motives are good and I understand his attempt to correct something that is wrong right now, but why not go after the bundle? Why not collect the full bundle and eliminate all of the pressures, eliminate to whatever extent it still exists-and it does to a considerable extent-the two solitudes on both sides of the river? Put them together. Certainly Hull is part of the national capital. No one can deny that. All you have to do is look at the thousands of civil servants crossing the bridges every morning, both ways, Put them into one jurisdiction. I do not believe the House of Commons should control that jurisdiction. You can certainly have a municipality with a municipal government that has representatives elected equally from all parts of Hull and from all parts of Ottawa. It would make a major contribution to national unity. I think also it might give those of us from the far outposts of this country a slightly better feeling about the national capital, knowing it was a separate jurisdiction that was not part of Ontario, that was not part of Quebec. By golly, let us have a district of one kind or another that belonged to all Canadians from whatever part of the country they may have come.

Mr. Speaker, on a personal basis I want to thank the good doctor, the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), for bringing this Bill forward. As I have studied the background of this Bill, he has singlehandedly taken this idea, developed it and nurtured it. He has sent out householders to people, and I gather now there is a substantial majority of people within Hull itself who are in favour of a National Capital Region. That is a real tribute to the Hon. Member. The former Member for Peace River, Mr. Ged Baldwin, worked for 15 years on freedom of information before that idea seeped through to all other Members of the House. I am sure each time the Hon. Member for Hull brings this Bill forward, there will be additional Members standing and saying they are in favour of it personally. I want to do that today, representing as I do a riding from southern Alberta where there is an enormous feeling of distance and isolation from Ottawa as part of Ontario and the capital. What we need is, as the Hon. Member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) said, a national capital with which we can all truly identify, that is not associated with the provincial politics and conflicts that arise and the great baggage that history brings to each of the Provinces vis-a-vis each other.

I wonder, though, if the Hon. Member has given any thought to whether at this time, were the Bill to be referred to a committee, were an official committee of the House to deal with it, it would not revive somehow the battle between the federal Government and the provincial Government of Quebec? I would say to the Hon. Member that if he were prepared to convene a like minded group of Members of Parliament who
